The wrong pair is 'Amar Shaikh - Art collector'.

Amar Shaikh was not an art collector. He was Shahir Amar Sheikh, a people's bard, whose powadas inspired activists during the Sanyukta Maharashtra Movement. The other three pairs are correct: Jal Cooper was an internationally acclaimed philatelist, Kusumagraj was a noted Marathi poet, and Anna Bhau Sathe was Lokshahir Anna Bhau Sathe, a people's bard.

Written sources are one of the main types of sources used to study history. They include newspapers, periodicals, reference books, encyclopedias, correspondence, diaries, government gazettes, documents in the archives and postage stamps. The place where historical documents are preserved is called 'Archives'; the main office of the National Archives of India is at New Delhi and it is the largest among the Archives in Asia. Newspapers are considered the fourth pillar of democracy and give us information about national and international affairs, politics, art, sports, literature and social and cultural affairs. Among the print media, the annual issues of the Publications Division of the Government of India, such as the reference book INDIA 2000, give authentic and trustworthy information. With the help of all these written sources we can write the history of modern India.

The Press Trust of India (PTI) is an important written source for modern Indian history. After 1953, it has been an important source of primary details of all important events and of articles on important subjects. PTI has provided reports, photographs and articles on financial and scientific issues to newspapers, and it has now started its online service. During the 1990s, PTI started using 'satellite broadcast' technology instead of tele-printers to send news all over the country. All this material is important for writing the history of modern India.

The Postal Department issues postage stamps on a wide variety of themes like political leaders, flowers, animals, birds, an event, or the silver, golden, diamond jubilees or the centenary, bicentenary and tercentenary of different events. By putting the people, creatures and occasions that the country values on its stamps, the department keeps a record of them for later generations, which is why postage stamps are a valuable repository of history. There have also been several changes in postage stamps since India became independent, and the variety in their sizes, the novelty in their subjects and their colour schemes reveal a lot to us about changing times. For example, the Indian government issued the 'Jal Cooper' stamp in 1977 in honour of the internationally acclaimed philatelist Jal Cooper, and that stamp is an important source for understanding his significant contribution to the field. Postage stamps do not reveal anything on their own, but a historian makes them speak.

Television, films and the internet are called 'audio-visual media', and many domestic and foreign television channels such as the History channel and the Discovery channel also come under this head. The Government of India started the Film and Television Institute of India (FTII) at Pune in 1960 with the purpose of providing public education. An institute called Indian News Review has produced various newsreels on important events in politics, social issues, art, sports and culture, and it has also produced documentaries on prominent social leaders, on people who have made major contributions for the country and about important locations in India. These news releases and documentaries record contemporary events as they happened, so they are useful for studying the history of modern India. A huge amount of information is also available on the internet and is used for studying history, but its truth and authenticity needs to be verified.
